query: Has the canopy vigour in my block dropped since December according to the satellite?
final_text:
No — it hasn't dropped. Since early December it has been steadily climbing: NDVI went from 0.57 (Dec 10) to 0.63 (Dec 30) and 0.66 (Jan 9), a gain of about +0.09 over the month. That's the expected pattern for a vine in berry growth, with the canopy still filling out toward full cover.

One thing to note: about 0.6 ha (roughly 12% of the block) reads below median vigour in the latest scene. It's not enough to flag field-wide stress, but worth a ground check of that zone — irrigation pressure at the drip drippers, or a nitrogen dip, are the usual candidates. NDRE (0.31) is normal for this stage, so chlorophyll status looks fine.

query: Mostre a evolução do NDVI do meu talhão nos últimos três meses.
My soil test says pH 8.1, organic matter 0.9%, P Olsen 6 ppm and K 120 ppm. What does it mean?
final_text:
Your test shows an **alkaline, low-phosphorus, low-organic-matter soil** with acceptable potassium — a typical profile for coastal sandy-loam vineyard soils in the Valparaíso region. Here's what each number means:

- **pH 8.1 (alkaline):** outside the 6.0–7.2 range grapevine prefers. At this pH, micronutrients — especially **iron and zinc** — become poorly available, so iron chlorosis (yellowing between veins) is a real risk even if soil levels are normal. It also limits nitrogen uptake and favors calcium-dominant conditions.
- **P Olsen 6 ppm (deficient):** low for vine; can limit root development, shoot vigor and fruit-set. At pH above 7.5, P ties up with calcium and the effective availability is even lower than the number suggests.
- **K 120 ppm (adequate):** within the moderate-to-sufficient range; no sign of K limitation.
- **MO 0.9% (very low):** poor buffer and water-holding capacity, and it's part of why the pH sits where it does — these sandy coastal soils are naturally high in carbonates.

In short: the main issues to manage are the alkalinity (which will require acidifying amendments such as elemental sulfur, applied well in advance) and the low P, plus keeping an eye on foliar Zn/Fe as the risk increases with pH.

query: Petiole analysis at bloom: N 0.6%, K 1.2%, Mg 0.25%, B 22 ppm. Is anything deficient?
final_text:
Yes — three values sit at or below the petiole critical range for grapevine at bloom: **N 0.6% (below the 2.5% minimum), K 1.2% (at the bottom of the 1.2–2.5% range)** and **B 22 ppm (below ~25 ppm)**. **Mg 0.25% is exactly at the lower edge** of normal — not yet a deficiency, but worth tracking since it can drift lower during fruit fill.

Two caveats before acting: petiole N and K are typically lowest at bloom because they're being remobilized to the young berries, so these readings are early warnings more than confirmations. A second sample 2–3 weeks later (cluster node, ~2 weeks post-bloom), plus a visual check for leaves showing interveinal yellowing (Mg/B) or narrow early-season leaves (N), would distinguish a real deficit from normal seasonal redistribution before you correct anything.

query: Mi análisis de hojas dio Mg 0,15% y Mn 18 ppm en uva de mesa. ¿Están bajos?
final_text:
Sí, ambos están por debajo del rango útil en fructificación: **Mg 0,15%** frente a un mínimo de 0,25% (se considera deficiencia crítica; rango 0,25–0,80%) y **Mn 18 ppm** frente a un mínimo recomendado de 20 ppm (rango 20–200 ppm). El Mg es el problema mayor de tu muestra; el Mn está apenas bajo.

En vid, un Mg bajo a эта... es decir, un Mg bajo a nivel de broTES... — corrección: a nivel de hoja en fructificación es compatible con problemas de tamaño de baya, coloración o caída de hojas, y suele coincidir con suelos de pH alto o exceso de K que reduce la disponibilidad de Mg. El Mn bajo puede asociarse a pH elevado o suelos mal drenados en Casablanca, aunque una sola muestra no confirma la causa: conviene revisar si los síntomas (hoja pequeña, clorosis) aparecen en toda la parcela o solo en sectores, y verificar que el pH del suelo esté dentro de rango.

Si decides corregir, el Mg es el que requiere acción inmediata por estar en nivel crítico; el Mn se puede acompañar en la misma estrategia. Eso lo dimensiona tu asesor con el análisis de suelo y la disponibilidad de fuentes (nitrato, sulfato o quelato según el caso).

query: How many hours should I run my drip lines next week to cover the crop water demand?
final_text:
Next week's crop demand for your Casablanca vineyard (berry growth, Kc 1.1, ET₀ ~5.2–6.1 mm/day from the forecast, no rain) works out to a **gross sheet of ~53 mm** at an 8-day interval, which is **2,665 m³ for your 5 ha** at 90% drip efficiency.

To convert that into drip hours you need your emitters' flow rate, which isn't in your field record. As an example: with **16 L/h emitters at 2 m × 3 m** (~8,300 plants), 2,665 m³ ÷ 133,000 L/h ≈ **~20 h total**, splittable into two 10 h runs spaced 3–4 days apart to respect the soil's moisture holding capacity on loam.

Tell me your actual emitter flow (L/h) and spacing, and I'll give you the exact runtime per application.

- **"Sentinel-2 vegetation indices and within-vineyard vigour variability"** (2022) — useful because RDI trials are increasingly validated with canopy NDVI/NDVI as a surrogate for water potential, which fits your field monitoring.
- **"Nitrogen management in drip-fertigated vineyards"** (2019) — relevant interaction to consider if you plan to pair RDI with fertigation.

The INIA library has a 2017 *Manual de riego en vides de la zona central* (biblioteca.inia.cl/fixture/inia-001) with Chilean-specific irrigation guidance for valley vineyards.

For context from the broader RDI literature you'll want to anchor on (not retrieved in this search): the foundational work is Jones and colleagues at UC Davis (Jones et al., including Jones 2004 in *American Journal of Enology and Viticulture*, and subsequent RDI trials) plus Howell, Goode and colleagues in Australia and California — the consistent finding in Cabernet specifically is that RDI applied from veraison through to ~2 weeks before harvest increases skin-to-musl ratio, anthocyanin and tannin concentration, while berry weight and yield drop ~20–40%, with fruit quality benefits generally outweighing the yield loss in premium wine grapes.

query: Busque artigos científicos sobre sensoriamento remoto do estresse hídrico em videiras.
final_text:
Aqui estão os estudos mais relevantes localizados (OpenAlex, 2015 em diante) sobre sensoriamento remoto e estresse hídrico em videira:

- **Sentinel-2 vegetation indices and within-vineyard vigour variability** (2022) — uso de índices multiespectrais Sentinel-2 para mapear variabilidade de vigor e identificar setores sob estresse dentro de vinhedos. [doi.org/10.9999/fixture.oa.002](https://doi.org/10.9999/fixture.oa.002)
- **Deficit irrigation strategies for wine grapes under a Mediterranean climate** (2021) — estratégias de riego deficitário em clima mediterrâneo (diretamente aplicável à região de Casablanca), com base em monitoramento vigora e necessidade hídrica. [doi.org/10.9999/fixture.oa.001](https://doi.org/10.9999/fixture.oa.001)

Nota: a literatura mais robusta sobre estresse hídrico por satélite em videira vem da **termografia infravermelha** (excesso de temperatura foliar, ST/canopy temperature anomaly) e dos índices NDVI/NDRE multiespectrais, já que o estresse hídrico se manifesta primeiro no fechamento estomático — folha 2–3 °C acima do ar já indica esse fechamento. Se quiser, posso buscar artigos específicos de sensores térmicos ou de SCL (Stomatal Conductance index, usado em programas como o VINEO/Prader).

El balance de agua de la temporada va en **−460 mm**, así que el déficit hídrico es real y sostenido, no un episodio puntual.

Sobre el riego deficitario en INIA, la búsqueda no devolvió un documento titulado específicamente "riego deficitario"; el más próximo es el **Manual de riego en vides de la zona central** (INIA, 2017, [enlace](https://biblioteca.inia.cl/fixture/inia-001)) y el **Boletín agroclimático del valle de Casablanca** (2024, [enlace](https://biblioteca.inia.cl/fixture/inia-003)). query: In general terms, what is evapotranspiration?
final_text:
Evapotranspiration (ET) is the total water movement from a field to the atmosphere: evaporation from the soil plus transpiration through the crop's leaves. It is the main driver of crop water demand — the amount of water you actually apply in irrigation.

There are two standard figures. **ET₀ (reference evapotranspiration)** is the demand of a reference grass surface under fully water-supplied conditions, computed from meteorology (temperature, radiation, humidity, wind) with the FAO Penman-Monteith equation. The **crop coefficient (Kc)** scales ET₀ to the actual crop and phenological stage: ETc = Kc × ET₀. In your vineyard, for example, a mature grapevine in berry growth has a Kc near 0.85, so its water needs are about 85% of ET₀.
